young.html: Imagine you are a sailor, lost at sea for months, food running out. Suddenly you see an island no map has ever shown. The people there are kind. They take care of you. And they have a secret: a great house full of scientists, finding out everything about nature, and using it to help everyone.

That is the story Francis Bacon told in New Atlantis, about 400 years ago. The island is called Bensalem. Its house of learning is called Salomon's House. Bacon described its deep caves and tall towers for studying weather, its gardens and zoos for studying plants and animals, its rooms for light and sound, and even machines for flying and for going under water. In his day, none of these existed.

young.name: gb-salomon
young.cap: Meet the workers of Salomon's House. Each has a different job. Press "Follow a discovery" to see how an idea travels from one group to the next.

young.html: Plan your own Salomon's House. Draw a map of a research island. What rooms would you build? A room for studying stars? For growing better vegetables? For inventing robots? Give each team a funny name, like Bacon did ("Merchants of Light", "Lamps"), and write what they do.

full.html: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), lawyer, statesman and philosopher of science (see the rung on his Novum Organum), left this short story unfinished. His chaplain William Rawley published it in 1627, the year after Bacon died, at the end of Bacon's book of natural history, Sylva Sylvarum. It was written in English, so we can read it in Bacon's own words.
It belongs to a family of books about imagined ideal places, after Thomas More's Utopia (1516). But where More was mostly interested in laws and property, Bacon's island is organized around research.

Bacon believed that knowledge of nature could relieve hunger, disease and toil, but that no one person could do the work: it needed many hands, organized, paid and lasting for generations. Universities taught old books; craftsmen kept their skills secret. He could argue for a new kind of institution, but a story let readers see one working.

A ship sailing from Peru toward China and Japan is blown off course and finds Bensalem. The islanders give the crew a hospital and food and refuse any payment. The visitors learn the island's history: an old king named Solamona founded a great college, and the island keeps itself hidden from the world while sending out secret travelers to learn from it. The islanders are Christians, by an event the story tells as a miracle; Bacon presents their faith and their science as living side by side. Near the end, one of the Fathers of Salomon's House receives the narrator and describes the house. The book stops in the middle of his speech, with the note "The rest was not perfected."

full.text: The end of our foundation is the knowledge of causes, and secret motions of things; and the enlarging of the bounds of human empire, to the effecting of all things possible.
full.author: Francis Bacon

full.html: The Father lists the house's "preparations and instruments": caves as deep as six hundred fathoms for studying cold and minerals, towers half a mile high for weather, lakes of salt and fresh water, orchards and gardens for breeding new plants, parks of animals, kitchens and furnaces, and houses for light, sound, smells, engines and mathematics.

full.text: We have also perspective-houses, where we make demonstrations of all lights and radiations; and of all colours … We procure means of seeing objects afar off; as in the heaven and remote places; and represent things near as afar off; and things afar off as near …
full.author: Francis Bacon

full.html: Bacon wrote this in the 1620s, when the telescope and the microscope were brand new. He also imagines "some degrees of flying in the air", boats that go under water, and ways to send sounds through pipes over long distances.

The research is split among teams. Twelve Merchants of Light travel abroad in secret to bring back books and experiments. Others collect experiments from books, from the crafts, and by trying new ones. Compilers arrange the results in tables. Benefactors look for practical uses. After meetings of the whole body, Lamps plan new, deeper experiments, Inoculators carry them out, and Interpreters of Nature raise the results into general laws.

full.name: gb-salomon
full.cap: Click any team to read its job, Bacon's name for it and a modern counterpart. Bacon's sequence is close to the tables of the Novum Organum: gather, arrange, use, test again, generalize.

full.title: Counting the Fellows
full.q: Bacon lists twelve Merchants of Light and three in each of the other eight teams. How many Fellows is that, and what fraction travel abroad?
full.a: 36 Fellows; one third of them travel.

full.text: But we do hate all impostures, and lies; insomuch as we have severely forbidden it to all our fellows, under pain of ignominy and fines, that they do not show any natural work or thing, adorned or swelling; but only pure as it is, and without all affectation of strangeness.
full.author: Francis Bacon

items: It inspired a real society. The founders of the Royal Society of London (1660) saw themselves as building something like Salomon's House. Its early historian, Thomas Sprat, and the poet Abraham Cowley both praised Bacon as their guide.

It is not a prophecy. Some of Bacon's "inventions" sound modern, but he was listing hopes, often vague ones. The value of the book is its picture of organized, funded, cooperative research, not its predictions.

Secrecy. Bacon's scientists decide which discoveries to publish and which to keep secret, even from the state. Real science, from the Royal Society's journal (1665) on, went the other way, toward open publication, though debates about secret research continue.

full.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

full.html: Kept: research as a team effort, supported by the public or by patrons over many years; labs, observatories, botanical gardens and museums; the link between science and practical benefit. National academies, research universities and government labs all follow, in their own ways, the pattern Bacon sketched. Changed: open publication and peer review replaced secrecy, and scientists now argue about results in public journals instead of in a closed house.

deep.html: "All things possible." The house aims at "the effecting of all things possible." Is that a noble goal or a dangerous one? Bacon's islanders keep some discoveries secret because they judge them too dangerous. Who should decide what science does and what it shares? These questions are still debated, and thoughtful people answer them differently.

Faith and science together. Bensalem's people pray before and after their work and give thanks for discoveries. Bacon presents science and Christian faith as allies. Compare Galileo's trouble with church authorities, and Kepler's prayer at the end of the Harmonies. Thinkers of that century held many different views on how the two relate.
Utopia and its cousins. Later stories imagined research societies too, some hopeful, some warning: Jonathan Swift mocked a foolish academy of projectors in Gulliver's Travels (1726), on this ladder.
Big questions. Why did Bacon tell this as a story instead of an argument? What makes an ideal society? Should a society be organized around learning?

questions: If you could add one room to Salomon's House, what would it study?
The islanders refused payment for helping the sailors. Why might Bacon have made them so generous?
Should scientists ever keep a discovery secret? Who should decide?
Bacon's story ends with "The rest was not perfected." How do you think it would have ended?
Which of Bacon's imagined inventions exist now? Which do you think he would be most amazed by?
